audience: undergraduate computer science; spoken explanation of 1-3 minutes

key_points.text: Overfitting is when a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise and random quirks, instead of the general pattern.
key_points.partial_if: says the model 'memorises' the data without contrasting it with the general pattern

key_points.text: Symptom: very good performance on the training data but clearly worse performance on new, unseen data (poor generalisation).
key_points.partial_if: mentions only good training accuracy or only poor test accuracy, not the gap

key_points.text: Causes: a model that is too complex for the amount of data (too many parameters or features), too little or noisy training data, or training for too long.
key_points.partial_if: names one cause vaguely, e.g. 'too much training'

key_points.text: Detection: compare training error with error on a held-out validation or test set, or use cross-validation; validation error rising while training error falls is the sign.
key_points.partial_if: says 'use test data' without explaining what to compare

key_points.text: Remedies: more data or data augmentation, a simpler model or fewer features, regularisation (e.g. L1/L2, dropout), early stopping, pruning.
key_points.partial_if: names only one remedy, or remedies without how they help

key_points.text: Contrast with underfitting (too simple, poor on both training and test data); overfitting corresponds to high variance in the bias-variance trade-off.
key_points.partial_if: mentions underfitting without explaining the difference

misconceptions.text: Overfitting means the model performs poorly on its training data (this is underfitting).
Higher training accuracy always means a better model, so training longer always helps.
Checking accuracy on the training data is enough to detect overfitting.
